proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof ("ψ is injective on V, because π(G(a) − y) = a"; "for a ∈ V, π∘DG(a) = id (differentiate π(G(a) − y) = a), so DG(a) = fderiv ℝ ψ a is injective") and the identity π∘DG(a₀) = id used in step 3. No dependencies.
1. (Injectivity on D.) If a, b ∈ D and g(a) = g(b), then a = π(g(a) − c) = π(g(b) − c) = b.
2. (Chain rule.) Fix a ∈ D. Since D is open and g is differentiable on D, g is differentiable at a, i.e. HasFDerivAt g (Dg(a)) a. Let h(b) := π(g(b) − c). The map b ↦ g(b) − c has derivative Dg(a) at a, and π is continuous linear (its own derivative), so by the chain rule HasFDerivAt h (π ∘ Dg(a)) a.
3. (h is the identity near a.) h(b) = b for every b in the open neighbourhood D of a, so h agrees with the identity map on a neighbourhood of a. The identity has derivative id_{ℝ^d}, hence HasFDerivAt h id_{ℝ^d} a (HasFDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq). By uniqueness of the Fréchet derivative (HasFDerivAt.unique), π ∘ Dg(a) = id_{ℝ^d}.
4. (Injective derivative.) Evaluating step 3 at u gives π(Dg(a)u) = u for every u ∈ ℝ^d. If Dg(a)u = Dg(a)w, then u = π(Dg(a)u) = π(Dg(a)w) = w. So Dg(a) is injective.
5. (Conclusion.) Steps 1, 3 and 4 give the three assertions. ∎
key_steps: π(g(a) − c) = a on D forces injectivity of g on D.
By the chain rule b ↦ π(g(b) − c) has derivative π ∘ Dg(a) at a ∈ D; it equals the identity near a, so π ∘ Dg(a) = id by uniqueness of derivatives.
π ∘ Dg(a) = id makes Dg(a) injective.
